assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Gel electrophoresis
items.clue: A technique for separating DNA fragments by length.

items.label: DNA polymerase
items.clue: The enzyme that assembles a new strand of DNA on a template strand.

items.label: DNA profiling
items.clue: The comparison of the patterns of DNA fragments produced from different individuals at a set of variable regions (markers).

items.label: DNA replication
items.clue: The production of exact copies of a DNA molecule, each with a base sequence identical to the original, before a cell divides.

questions.stem: During replication, a section of a template strand with the base sequence TACGGA is copied. Which statement describes the new strand built on this section?

options.text: Its sequence is TACGGA, an exact copy of the template strand it was assembled on.
Its sequence is ATGCCT, the complement of the template, held to it by hydrogen bonds.
Its sequence is AUGCCU, because uracil replaces thymine in each newly made strand.
Its sequence is ATGCCT, held to the template by covalent bonds made by DNA polymerase.

questions.stem: What is the role of helicase in DNA replication?

options.text: It cuts through the sugar–phosphate backbone so that the two strands can come apart.
It adds free nucleotides to each exposed template strand to assemble the two new strands.
It forms the hydrogen bonds that hold each new nucleotide to its complementary base on the template.
It unwinds the double helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds between the two strands.

questions.explanation: Helicase unwinds the helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, separating the strands so that each can serve as a template for DNA polymerase.

questions.stem: What is the role of the primers in the polymerase chain reaction?

options.text: They break the hydrogen bonds between the two strands so that the polymerase can reach the template.
They only speed the reaction up, because Taq polymerase could begin a new strand at any point along the bare template.
They bind to sequences either side of the target, giving the polymerase a start point and defining the region copied.
They are identical in sequence to the section being copied, so that the polymerase has an exact copy of it to work from.

questions.stem: A PCR reaction starts with 10 double-stranded DNA molecules of the target section. How many double-stranded molecules of the target are present after 3 complete cycles?
questions.explanation: Every molecule is copied in every cycle, so the number doubles each cycle: 10 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 10 × 2³ = 80.

questions.stem: During replication, how does DNA polymerase add each new nucleotide to the strand it is building?

options.text: It joins the 3' hydroxyl of the incoming nucleotide to the 5' terminal of the growing strand, so that the strand grows in the 3' to 5' direction.
It adds to whichever terminal faces the fork, so both new strands grow in the same direction as the replication fork moves.
It forms hydrogen bonds between the incoming nucleotide and the template base, which then hold the nucleotide in the strand.
It joins the 5' phosphate of the incoming nucleotide to the 3' terminal of the growing strand, so the strand grows in the 5' to 3' direction.

questions.stem: What is the function of DNA polymerase I in prokaryotic DNA replication?

options.text: It synthesizes most of the new DNA on both strands, being the first polymerase to act at the fork.
It joins the sugar–phosphate backbones of adjacent Okazaki fragments to make one continuous lagging strand.
It removes the RNA nucleotides of each primer and replaces them with DNA nucleotides, filling the gap.
It synthesizes the short DNA primer that DNA polymerase III needs at the start of each fragment.
